column2: Also on the authority of Abū Dharr (may Allah be pleased with him) that some of the Companions of the Messenger of Allah (Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace) said to the Prophet (Allah the Exalted bless him and his family and grant them peace):
“O Messenger of Allah, the people of wealth have gone off with the rewards: they pray as we pray, they fast as we fast, and they give in charity from the surplus of their wealth.”

He said: “Has Allah not given you things with which to give charity? Every tasbīḥah is a charity, every takbīrah is a charity, every taḥmīdah is a charity, every tahlīlah is a charity, enjoining good is a charity, forbidding evil is a charity, and in the intimate relations of one of you there is a charity.” They said:
“O Messenger of Allah, does one of us fulfil his desire and have a reward for it?”
He said: “Do you not see that if he were to put it in something unlawful, he would bear a sin for it? Likewise, if he puts it in what is lawful, he has a reward for it.” Reported by Muslim.
In the list of charities the printed text repeats تهليلة where تكبيرة (“takbīrah”) is expected, as the commentary's own gloss on «بكل تكبيرة صدقة» shows; the translation follows the intended wording.
Nāsan (“some”): they were the poor among the Emigrants, as in the other narration.

“Of the Companions of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ”: aṣḥāb is the plural of ṣāḥib in the sense of ṣaḥābī (Companion), who is one who met Muḥammad ﷺ after his prophethood and before his death, believing in him, and died in that state, even if he did not see him, like Ibn Umm Maktūm.

Al-duthūr (“the people of wealth”): with ḍammah on the dāl and with the thāʾ; plural of dathr, with fatḥah then sukūn, meaning abundant wealth. “From the surplus of their wealth”: from their wealth that exceeds their needs.
Taṣṣaddaqūna (“to give charity”): the narration of this word has both the ṣād and the dāl doubled, though linguistically the ṣād may be light.
“And every takbīrah is a charity (ṣadaqah)”: ṣadaqah is narrated in the nominative and the accusative; the nominative as a new clause,
and the accusative as coordinated with “inna bi-kulli tasbīḥatin ṣadaqatan”; and likewise what follows it.
Buḍʿ (“intimate relations”): with ḍammah then sukūn; it is used for intercourse and for the private part itself, and either may be meant here.
Wizr (“a sin”): a burden of sin.
The Companions' eagerness for righteous deeds and the strength of their desire for good, such that one of them would grieve over good he could not do which another was able to do,
as the poor grieved over missing the charity of wealth that the rich were able to give.

Charity is not restricted to wealth; rather, charity in other forms may be better, such as enjoining good and forbidding evil, which is calling to obedience to Allah and restraining from disobedience to Him,

and that is better than benefiting [others] with wealth; likewise teaching beneficial knowledge, teaching the Qurʾān, removing harmful things from the road, striving to bring benefit to people and ward off harm from them, and supplicating for the Muslims and seeking forgiveness for them.
The virtue of saying subḥān Allāh, Allāhu akbar, al-ḥamdu lillāh and lā ilāha illā Allāh, and of enjoining good and forbidding evil.
One seeking a ruling may ask about some of the evidence that is unclear to him, if he knows that the one asked does not dislike that and if there is no bad manners in it.
A scholar may mention the evidence for some unclear questions, and a muftī may point out the evidence in brief.

Bringing the intention to mind in permissible matters, and that they become acts of obedience through a sincere intention, such as intending by intercourse to fulfil the wife's right and to live with her in the kindly manner Allah has commanded, or seeking a righteous child, or keeping himself chaste, or keeping his wife chaste, and other good aims.
The permissibility of analogy (qiyās). What is transmitted from the Salaf in censure of analogy refers to analogy that clashes with a text.
